children: The revised cap will apply through March 2027, while APM gas for ONGC and Oil India remains subject to a separate USD 7/MMBtu ceiling

The government has raised the ceiling price for natural gas produced from difficult fields, including deepwater, ultra-deepwater and high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) discoveries, to USD 9.89 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) for the six months beginning 1 October 2026. The revised ceiling, up from USD 8.90 per MMBtu, will remain in force until 31 March 2027, according to a notification issued by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.

The new ceiling applies to technically challenging offshore resources, including Reliance Industries and BP’s KG-D6 block in the Krishna-Godavari basin. Producers from these fields have marketing and pricing freedom under the government’s policy framework, but the prices they charge remain subject to the government-notified ceiling.

The increase could provide some relief to producers developing technically challenging offshore gas resources, where exploration and production costs are generally higher than those associated with mature onshore and legacy fields. The separate pricing regime for difficult fields was introduced to encourage investment and accelerate the development of hydrocarbon resources that are more complex and expensive to produce.

Separately, the government has notified an administered price mechanism (APM) gas price of USD 11.22 per MMBtu for October for nomination fields operated by Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) and Oil India (OIL). However, the applicable ceiling means the actual price remains capped at USD 7 per MMBtu.

APM gas is supplied to priority sectors, including city gas distribution, fertiliser manufacturing and power generation. Changes in the price of this gas can therefore affect input costs for industries that depend on domestic supplies.

For gas produced from new wells in ONGC and OIL’s nomination blocks, producers are permitted a 10 per cent premium over the prevailing APM price, subject to the applicable ceiling. With the APM ceiling at USD 7 per MMBtu for October, the effective price for gas from new wells can reach USD 7.70 per MMBtu, according to PPAC.

The premium is intended to encourage ONGC and OIL to invest in developing additional reserves and bringing new production on stream, while gas from older producing fields remains subject to the existing ceiling.

In April 2023, the government shifted the pricing mechanism for legacy gas to a formula linked to 10 per cent of the monthly average crude oil import price, subject to a floor and ceiling. The ceiling was initially fixed at USD 6.50 per MMBtu. Following a two-year freeze, it was raised by USD 0.25 annually, reaching USD 6.75 per MMBtu in April 2025 and USD 7 per MMBtu in April 2026.

Natural gas remains an important feedstock for fertiliser production and is also used for power generation and by city gas distributors supplying compressed natural gas (CNG) and piped natural gas (PNG). The latest revision raises the price ceiling available to producers of difficult-field gas while maintaining separate pricing limits for gas from nomination and legacy fields.
